newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says thousands of Zaireans join refugee exodus.
newsitem.headline: UN says thousands of Zaireans join refugee exodus.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency said on Wednesday that thousands of Zaireans had joined an exodus of some 220,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees fleeing clashes in eastern Zaire.
Zairean troops are fighting ethnic Tutsis in the volatile region in what Sadako Ogata, U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees has said could degenerate into a "humanitarian catastrophe".
"Thousands of local Zaireans are fleeing," UNHCR spokesman Ron Redmond said. "There are reports of fighting. There are rumours of fighting that are also causing people to move."
The fighting in east Zaire's Uvira area in Africa's troubled Great Lakes region pits Zairean troops against Tutsi immigrants, known as Banyamulenge, and native Zaireans.
Redmond said the UNHCR had no deathtoll from the Uvira fighting. Aid workers said local staff had asked for 78 body bags and had spoken of 60 wounded, mostly civilians.

He said between 70,000 and 100,000 Burundian and Rwandan Hutu refugees as well as local Zaireans displaced by the violence were on the move in Bukavu area, 75 km (50 miles) north of Uvira. Many were hiding in the bush and nearby hills.
The U.N. had no details on the intensity of fighting between Zairean forces and the ethnic Tutsi rebels.
Eastern Zaire has been gripped by unrest since the 1994 massacres and civil war in Rwanda sent more than a million Hutu refugees streaming in, stoking ethnic rivalry in the area.
Elsewhere, Redmond said UNHCR had no further details on Tuesday reports from the Zairean military of attacks near Rwandan Hutu refugee camps in Goma region to the north.
Redmond said field workers were counting 1,500 new arrivals per hour on the outskirts of Bukavu on Tuesday.
Refugees told the UNHCR that one of the camps in Uvira region, Kamanyola, had been overrun by Tutsi rebels but UNHCR had no details, he said.

Kamanyola and several other camps in Uvira region are home to some of the most extremist Hutu militiamen who played a key role in the Hutu-led genocide of more than half a million ethnic Tutsis and Hutu moderates in Rwanda.

The refugees, including many mass killers, are fed and watered by U.N. agencies while Hutu militia in the camps launch cross-border raids into Rwanda at will, killing genocide survivors, laying mines and attacking military targets.
Diplomats and aid workers fear the armies of neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi, both dominated by Tutsis, might be drawn in on the side of the Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels.

Rwanda's minority Tutsi rulers feel prosecuted, outnumbered and surrounded by majority Hutus and some members of the Tutsi-led army say privately they are prepared to take matters into their own hands. Many soldiers of the army, which took power after the genocide, grew up in neighbouring Zaire, Uganda and Burundi.
